title: Candidates Are Signing a Pact Promising Action on Data Centers and AI Safety
gist: Data centers and AI have become a genuinely bipartisan 2026 midterm wedge issue: over 15 candidates have signed an 'AI Pact' targeting tax breaks and unregulated AI, while both Democratic and Republican governors (Shapiro, Abbott) are publicly reversing course toward stricter data-center oversight.

themes.theme: Data centers as a cross-partisan electoral flashpoint

insights.claim: Independent US Senate candidate Dan Osborn found instant, complete agreement with a self-described 'hardcore MAGA' voter in Nebraska the moment the conversation turned to AI and data centers, despite having little else in common with him.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Illustrates that opposition to unchecked data center growth is becoming a rare issue with genuine cross-partisan pull in swing states, raising political risk for hyperscaler siting and subsidy deals regardless of which party controls a given statehouse.
insights.quote: Boy, right away, we were in lockstep, 100 percent agreement.
insights.locator: opening anecdote about Osborn's town hall

insights.claim: More than 15 candidates for office across multiple states have signed the 'AI Pact,' a five-point pledge including mandatory safety reviews for AI models, support for an AI-profit worker dividend, and ensuring consumers and companies can sue over AI-caused harms.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: A growing slate of candidates campaigning on binding AI liability and safety-review commitments signals rising legislative risk for AI developers and infrastructure operators if these candidates win.

insights.claim: The AI Pact deliberately avoids calling for an outright data center moratorium, instead asking candidates to support banning 'tax breaks, backroom deals, and excessive energy usage' for data centers, a calibrated floor meant to keep labor-aligned candidates on board.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: The likely near-term policy fight is over tax incentives and ratepayer cost allocation for data centers rather than outright bans, directly relevant to hyperscalers' effective tax rates and utility rate cases.
insights.quote: support policies that would ban tax breaks, backroom deals, and excessive energy usage for data centers
insights.locator: paragraph on the pledge's specific language

insights.claim: Progressive strategist Alexander McCoy says swing-seat candidates are torn between wanting data-center construction jobs now and fearing AI's broader disruption of workers in their districts, which is producing deliberately vague, jobs-friendly campaign language rather than outright opposition.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Expect most swing-district candidates to hedge (support jobs, oppose subsidies/energy costs) rather than adopt hard anti-data-center positions, moderating near-term legislative risk outside of the most opposition-heavy districts.
insights.quote: Candidates in swing seats are laser-focused on affordability, creating jobs, and lowering costs.

themes.theme: Governors reversing course on data centers

insights.claim: Texas Republican Governor Greg Abbott initiated a temporary moratorium on data center construction this month after saying data centers have 'dug their own grave' in the state, a reversal from his prior pro-development stance.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: A moratorium in Texas, a top state for AI data center growth, is a concrete policy action (not just rhetoric) that directly threatens the construction timelines of planned hyperscaler capacity in the state.

insights.claim: Pennsylvania Democratic Governor Josh Shapiro, previously supportive of data center development, has also taken major public steps to reassure voters he is regulating the industry.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: The backlash is pulling in previously pro-development Democratic governors as well as Republicans, suggesting the political pressure to regulate data centers is broad-based rather than confined to one party.

insights.claim: Texas AG and Senate candidate Ken Paxton released a data center policy plan that would make data centers legally liable for chatbots that 'undermine children's safety,' extending liability exposure beyond AI model developers to the infrastructure operators hosting them.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: A novel liability theory that reaches data center operators (not just AI labs) would expand the legal exposure surface for data center owners/operators and REITs, not just AI companies themselves.
insights.locator: paragraph on Paxton's data center plan

insights.claim: The Trump administration is developing a voluntary safety-review framework for AI models, has discussed a worker dividend from AI profits reportedly pitched by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, and has encouraged AI companies and utilities to sign a voluntary pledge protecting ratepayers from data-center-driven electricity price increases.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: The likely near-term federal response is voluntary/soft frameworks rather than binding legislation, meaning enforcement risk in the near term is more likely to show up at the state and utility-rate-case level than in federal law.
insights.locator: paragraph on White House AI safety review and ratepayer pledge

insights.claim: AI Pact organizer Daniel Lobo-Lewis dismisses the Trump administration's voluntary AI and data center measures as insufficient, arguing the administration would not actually pursue mandatory safety reviews or end nationwide data center tax breaks.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Frames a real gap between voluntary federal gestures and binding regulation, suggesting investors should not treat the administration's voluntary pledges as durable protection against future stricter state-level rules.
insights.quote: I can't imagine [the Trump administration] would actually want to do mandatory safety reviews for models, or nationwide tax breaks for data center construction
insights.locator: Lobo-Lewis quote near end of article

insights.claim: Senator Bernie Sanders was among the first politicians to explicitly link AI safety to data centers when he proposed, in March, a national moratorium on data center construction until Congress passes AI safeguard legislation, a position other candidates have since echoed.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Sanders' early moratorium proposal functioned as a template that a growing number of down-ballot candidates are now adopting, suggesting this framing could keep spreading into 2026 legislative sessions.

themes.theme: Is this really about AI, or about local impacts?

insights.claim: Some polling cited in the piece suggests environmental worries about data centers (noise, land use, water and power consumption) still far outrank AI-specific concerns among the public, raising questions about how tightly data center opposition is actually connected to AI safety fears.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: If opposition is driven more by local environmental/nuisance impact than AI fears specifically, infrastructure-level mitigations (noise, water, ratepayer protections) could defuse political risk more easily than genuine AI-specific regulation would.
insights.locator: paragraph near end on polling and pundit skepticism

insights.claim: Representative Justin Pearson built national political prominence opposing pollution from SpaceX's data center operations near Memphis, and Will Lawrence won a competitive Michigan primary in a district with active data center opposition, showing anti-data-center positioning can now be a winning primary strategy.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Primary wins built on anti-data-center platforms indicate the issue has real electoral potency, likely encouraging more candidates to adopt similar positions in 2026 races.

insights.claim: Osborn links data center opposition to the broader Big Tech privacy backlash, explicitly connecting it to proliferation of Flock automatic license plate reader cameras, suggesting the anti-data-center coalition may be fusing with the separate backlash against surveillance technology.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: A merged narrative linking data centers, AI, and surveillance tech backlash could broaden the political coalition and durability of anti-Big-Tech regulatory pressure across multiple sectors at once.
insights.locator: closing paragraphs on Osborn and Flock cameras
